# Slop patterns

v2: v1 generic patterns + blader/humanizer 3.1.0 additions (MIT, commit 225a6f39; reworded). v3: agency-wide. Vertical slop lists moved to `/home/box/agent-data/workflows/tharros-shared-references/references/verticals/<vertical>/pack.md`; client-specific examples live in `/home/box/agent-data/workflows/tharros-shared-references/references/clients/<client>/voice.md` or the profile's Voice section. Examples below mix verticals.

Use this file for detect and edit. Quote the offending line. Severity = how much it hurts trust or delays the ask.

`high` — blocks the sale or sounds like every other site in the category  
`med` — dilutes voice or hides the fact  
`low` — tidy later; one instance in a long piece

One binary contrast in 1,500 words is `low`. Five stacked kickers in an email are `high`.

## Structural patterns

### Binary contrasts
Smell: “This is not X. It’s Y.” / “The question isn’t X, it’s Y.” / “It’s not just a mini-split. It’s a comfort system.”
Fix: State Y. “We size the heads and the outdoor together, then tell you what ships.”

### Throat-clearing openers
Smell: “Here’s the thing,” “Let me be clear,” “I’ll be honest,” “The uncomfortable truth is.”
Fix: Start with the point. Keep “I’ll be honest” only if the next clause is a real limitation (lead time, freight, not DIY).

### Faux-insight setups
Smell: “What nobody tells you,” “The part everyone misses,” “Here’s what most buyers get wrong.”
Fix: Make the claim. “Outdoor capacity is not the sum of the indoor nameplates.”

### Colon reveals
Smell: “The best part: it just works.” / “The secret: we design first.”
Fix: Normal sentence. Colons are for lists, labels, hours, phone labels — not fake drama.

### Superficial analysis
Smell: trailing “highlighting,” “underscoring,” “reflecting,” “showcasing.”
Fix: Mechanism or consequence. Not “highlighting our commitment to comfort.” Yes “so the bedroom and the sunroom can run off one outdoor.”

### Importance puffery
Smell: “marks a pivotal moment,” “stands as a testament,” “plays a vital role,” “underscores its significance.”
Fix: The fact. “This is a hyper-heat outdoor, not a cooling-only unit.”

### Interpretive metadiscourse
Smell: “The key point is,” “As you can see,” “This distinction matters,” “Here’s why that matters,” redundant “In other words.”
Fix: Delete the tour-guide line. If the point is unclear, add a fact, not a label.

### Weasel attribution
Smell: “Experts agree,” “studies show,” “customers everywhere are switching,” “widely regarded as.”
Fix: Name the source or cut it. Do not invent Energy Star stats, review counts, or “most popular.”

### Fake-strong verbs
Smell: “serves as a centralized hub for comfort,” “enables users to achieve,” “provides a comprehensive solution.”
Fix: What the unit does. “The wall head cools the addition. The outdoor sits on a pad or wall bracket.”

### Synonym cycling
Smell: “system” then “solution” then “setup” then “comfort platform” for the same object.
Fix: Repeat the right word — system, head, outdoor, line set, draft, quote.

### Negative listing
Smell: “Not a window unit. Not a portable. A ductless system.”
Fix: Say what it is.

### Dramatic fragmentation
Smell: “That’s it. That’s the whole thing.” / “Quiet. Efficient. Done.”
Fix: Complete sentences. Fragments are allowed only if they sound like us on the phone, not like an ad stack.

### Robotic rhythm
Smell: same sentence shape every time; three-beat paragraphs; stacked punchy fragments.
Fix: Vary only when it helps. Do not force symmetry.

### Rhetorical setups
Smell: “What if I told you…”, “Think about it:”, “Plot twist:”, “Question? Answer.”
Fix: Drop the bit.

### Fake-profound kickers
Smell: “The future of comfort isn’t coming. It’s already here.” Cute metaphor endings.
Fix: Delete. Do not rewrite into a better metaphor. End on the ask, the freight fact, or the phone number.

### Summary-recap endings
Smell: “In conclusion,” “Ultimately,” “Overall,” plus a paragraph that restates the page.
Fix: Last concrete point or next action.

### Formatting slop
Smell: emoji headings, mid-sentence **bold** for emphasis, bullets that should be two sentences, a heading over a two-line section, markdown `###` inside a short email.
Fix: Format follows the container. Emails and SMS are prose.

### Em-dash default
Smell: dash clusters, dash as rhythm crutch in every sentence.
Fix: Prefer comma, period, or parenthesis. One dash in a long piece is fine if it beats the alternative.

### Whether-you’re merism
Smell: “Whether you’re a homeowner or a contractor…”
Fix: Pick the reader or split the page. Segments buy differently (homeowner vs contractor, first order vs reorder, solo operator vs multi-truck shop).

### From-X-to-Y sweep
Smell: “From studios to whole homes, from DIY to pro…”
Fix: Name the job this page is for.

### Rule-of-three padding
Smell: three parallel clauses with no extra meaning.
Fix: Keep the one that earns the sentence.

### Invented framework
Smell: “The 4 pillars of comfort.” “Our 3-step journey.”
Fix: Keep numbered structure only if the user asked for steps or the draft already had a real process (size → match → quote → ship).

### Good-news / bad-news
Smell: fake tension before a simple fact.
Fix: State the fact. “Freight is extra on this condenser. Parcel on the heads.”

### Soft ask / hope-this-helps
Smell: “Feel free to reach out.” “Let us know if you have any questions.” “Hope this helps!”
Fix: The next action. “Call [brand phone] with the room list and square footage.”

### Both-sides symmetry
Smell: every limitation gets a matching shiny pro so the paragraph stays balanced.
Fix: Keep the real tradeoff (DIY vs warranty, repair vs replace, freight sticker, self-serve vs managed plan).

### Product anthropomorphism
Smell: “The system understands your comfort needs.”
Fix: What it does at a setpoint, in a room, at an outdoor temperature.

### Confidence with no object
Smell: “The data is clear.” “The market has spoken.” “Customers are making the switch.”
Fix: A number we actually have, or cut.

### Workshop anecdote
Smell: “I used to think mini-splits were only for additions. Then I realized…”
Fix: Keep only if the first-person detail is specific and checkable. Otherwise state the use case.

### Portable competitor filler
Smell: any line that could run on a competitor's site unchanged.
Fix: Attach a client fact from `/home/box/agent-data/workflows/tharros-shared-references/references/clients/<client>/profile.md` (service area, real process, catalog, protected phone). The client's `voice.md` or Voice section may list the specific competitors and facts to use.

## Humanizer additions (v2)

### Arguing with no one
Smell: "This isn't about price." / "To be clear," / "Don't get me wrong," / "You might think you need a new system, but..." when nobody raised it.
Fix: State the claim. Keep an objection only if the customer actually raises it (from call notes, reviews, or the brief).

### Repeated sentence openings
Smell: "We install. We service. We warranty." / three sentences in a row starting with "Our".
Fix: Merge, or start with the action. Deliberate rhythm in a headline is fine.

### Stacked qualifiers
Smell: "could potentially help possibly lower bills."
Fix: One qualifier the source supports: "may lower your bill." Keep legal, safety, and rebate-eligibility caveats. *Weak alone.*

### Vague association
Smell: "associated with [manufacturer]," "connected to top brands," "tied to local rebates."
Fix: Name the relationship the client profile gives (authorized dealer, the exact dealer-tier name, eligible under program X). A dealer tier or badge must be current: run `claims-check` (badge currency, co-op rules). If the brief does not say, keep it vague rather than invent a status.

### Knowledge-limit residue
Smell: "as of my last update," "based on available information," "details are not widely documented," "likely founded in the 1990s."
Fix: Delete, or state what the source does not show. Never guess to fill the gap.

### Heading repeated in the first sentence
Smell: "## Financing" then "Financing is available."
Fix: Cut the echo. Start with the terms or the ask.

### Writing about the document
Smell: "This page covers...," "the table below compares," "we flagged anything we could not confirm."
Fix: Say the thing. Keep a caveat only if it changes what the reader should do.

### Re-explaining what the reader knows (replies, client emails, quote follow-ups)
Smell: a reply that restates the customer's problem, the diagnosis, and the evidence before reaching the decision.
Fix: Lead with the decision and the next step. Keep one fact they lack and any link they need.

### Hyphenated pairs after the noun (*weak alone*)
Smell: "the install is high-quality," "the process is well-documented."
Fix: Drop the hyphen after the noun ("high quality"). Keep it before the noun.

## Portable-claim slop (every client)

Cut or replace with a specific, sourced fact from the client profile:

- "look no further," "we go above and beyond," "your satisfaction is our priority"
- "peace of mind" (when nothing specific backs it)
- "family-owned and operated" (unless true, in the profile, and specific: whose family, since when)
- "#1 in [city or category]" (unless sourced and dated; `claims-check`)

Vertical slop lists (load the one the profile names): `/home/box/agent-data/workflows/tharros-shared-references/references/verticals/home-service/pack.md` (trade slop), `/home/box/agent-data/workflows/tharros-shared-references/references/verticals/ecommerce-dtc/pack.md` (e-com slop), `/home/box/agent-data/workflows/tharros-shared-references/references/verticals/saas-b2b/pack.md` (SaaS and agency slop).

## Empty words

Cut when they add atmosphere, not meaning:

delve, foster, leverage, utilize, facilitate, empower, streamline, robust, cutting-edge, paradigm shift, game changer, this is huge, this changes everything, tapestry, realm, beacon, multifaceted, meticulous, intricate, paramount, transformative, elevate, embark, supercharge, harness, ever-evolving, unlock, next-level, curated, ecosystem. Vertical additions live in the vertical pack.

Keep robust / leverage only when they are the precise technical word, not atmosphere. Often-empty adverbs (just, actually, honestly, simply) stay when they are how a salesperson talks. Cut them when they delay the point.

Phrases to cut when they delay the point:

it’s worth noting, it’s important to note, at the end of the day, when it comes to, at its core, in today’s world, in the age of, the reality is, the truth is, in terms of, with regard to, in order to, going forward, in this article, let’s dive in, let’s break this down.

## Before / after (examples by vertical)

Home service. Before: `It’s not just a new AC. It’s a whole new way to think about comfort.`
After: `A two-stage system runs longer at low speed, so upstairs stays closer to the setpoint. Call [brand phone] and we’ll size it.`

Home service. Before: `What nobody tells you: sizing is everything.`
After: `A west-facing room with a lot of glass needs more cooling than its square footage says. Send the room list before you buy.`

Local service. Before: `Your comfort is our top priority, and we go above and beyond.`
After: `We call 30 minutes before we arrive and put down floor covers. [confirm with owner]`

E-com. Before: `Elevate your comfort with our curated collection of premium systems.`
After: `Lennox condensers and matching coils. Call and we'll size it, then you buy online. [confirm brands with owner]`

SaaS. Before: `Supercharge your growth with our all-in-one, AI-powered platform.`
After: `See which ads brought in booked jobs this week, in one screen. [confirm feature is live with owner]`

Client-specific before/after examples live in `/home/box/agent-data/workflows/tharros-shared-references/references/clients/<client>/voice.md`.

## When not to act

Leave a watched phrase alone inside a quotation, a product or program name, a review quote, or a passage that discusses the phrase. Sign-offs on a letter predate chatbots. One tell is not proof; several together are. Keep the details that carry the writer's voice: a real street name, an odd customer quote, a mixed feeling, a genuine aside.

## Not adopted from humanizer

- §8 blanket em/en dash ban. The no-slop rule stands: dashes optional, clusters banned. Running both produces flip-flopping edits.
- §21 curly quotes (cosmetic; CMSs and Docs auto-curl).
- In-place file mode (this skill returns drafts; the owner pastes).
